newsitem.title: VATICAN: Cuban exiles bring anti-Castro campaign to Pope.
newsitem.headline: Cuban exiles bring anti-Castro campaign to Pope.

text.p: Cuban exiles brought their anti-communist campaign to the Vatican on Wednesday days before a probable historic meeting between Pope John Paul and communist leader Fidel Castro.

"Viva Cuba Libre" (Long Live Free Cuba) and "Queremos Libertad para Cuba" (We Want Freedom for Cuba), they shouted as the Pope acknowledged their presence among pilgrims in the Vatican's audience hall.
Some of the 80 Cuban exiles in the group held up photographs, apparently of political prisoners.
The Miami-based exiles carried a hand-painted mantle dotted with signatures and messages by nearly 100 political prisoners.
They draped it over an 81-year-old wheelchair-bound woman, Dalia Santana, who was brought to the front of the audience hall and greeted by the Pope at his weekly general audience.
"I pray for Cuba every day," the Pope told her.
The mantle was decorated with the Cuban and American flags and an image of the Virgin Mary watching over exiles fleeing the island in small boats and rafts.
The Pope is expected to meet Castro for the first time later this week, an encounter that could lead to the first Papal trip to the communist island.
Castro, the world's longest serving communist leader and icon of the international left, is expected in Rome in the early hours of Friday for the U.N.-sponsored World Food Summit.
The Cuban group's participation in the Papal audience was part of what they call a "Pilgrimage of Pain" to protest against alleged human rights abused in Cuba on the eve of Castro's visit to Rome.
One of the participants was Mario Chanes, who said he spent 30 years as a political prisoner in Cuba.

The Vatican has said the 76-year-old Polish Pope will give an audience to Castro, an atheist whose government has sometimes testy relations with the Roman Catholic Church, if the Cuban leader asks for one.
The meeting is expected to to followed by a historic trip by the Pope to Cuba, the only Spanish- or Portuguese-speaking Latin American country the stridently anti-communist Pontiff has not visited.
Vatican sources say an eventual Papal trip to Cuba would probably take place next year.

The group at Wednesday's audience included relatives of four men killed last February when Cuba shot down two small planes operated by the Miami-based Brothers to the Rescue. They were looking for Cubans trying to reach the United States by boat.
Cuba said the planes were in its airspace. The United States said they were over international waters and condemned Havana for shooting down civilian aircraft.
